title: Why Telegram ignores legal charges in Iran and Russia: cut every link so no one has leverage
summary: Durov explains why prosecutions in Iran and Russia don't hurt Telegram: the company has no legal presence there and severs any local link (like the outsourced spam contractor Telegraf) so regulators have nothing to target. He argues restrictive laws in an open, connected world mostly hurt the countries that pass them.

principles.text: Keep no legal presence in hostile jurisdictions, so regulators have no leverage over you.
principles.quote: Luckily, we don't have any legal presence in any of these countries.

principles.text: Be ready to cut all personal and business ties to places that pressure you over user privacy.
principles.quote: We are always ready to cut all our personal and business links to such places so that they don't have any leverage on us.

principles.text: Restrictive laws backfire in an open world: they drive talent and companies out and damage the local economy.
principles.quote: If you pass archaic laws that limit freedoms, all you'll end up doing is killing your own economy.

principles.text: Serve users in restrictive markets from jurisdictions that respect freedom rather than from inside the market.
principles.quote: Until then, we'll continue providing secure messaging to users in these markets from places that respect freedom.

principles.text: Blocking a product on their territory doesn't always work; privacy and freedom prevail in the long run.
principles.quote: They can try to block us on their territory, but, as I've shown in my previous post about China, even this won't always help them.

principles.text: Accept personal costs (like travel bans) as a small price for defending core principles.
principles.quote: Not being able to occasionally drop by is not great, but a small price to pay considering the matters at stake.
